title: Bird species centroids moved about 35 km north on 1,471 fixed North American survey routes from 1975-1989 to 2010-2024, at about 14% of the isotherm shift and not in proportion to it
abstract: Question: did the breeding ranges of North American bird species move north, and did the shifts follow warming? Approach: we used 51,283 standard Breeding Bird Survey runs on 1,471 routes with at least 5 runs in each of 1975-1989, 1992-2006 and 2010-2024. A fixed route set removes changes in route coverage. For 379 species we calculated abundance-weighted centroid latitude and occupancy-based north and south edges. We compared shifts with the isotherm shift from NOAA GHCN_CAMS May-July temperature. We used a 2-degree spatial block bootstrap and a year-label permutation test. Results: from 1975-1989 to 2010-2024, the mean centroid moved 34.5 km north (95% CI 20.6 to 45.8; 63% of species north; permutation p = 0.001). The shift was north in the East (21.8 km) and the West (34.0 km), and occurred mostly after 2005. Observation bias: the centroid of all birds together also moved 19.0 km north. A route-normalized centroid, which removes all route-level count changes, gave a smaller shift of 21.9 km (13.9 to 30.2), still north in both regions. Warming was 0.88 C and the mean isotherm shift was 268 km, so the tracking ratio was 0.14 (0.09 to 0.18), or 0.08 route-normalized. Species with larger isotherm shifts did not move further (correlation -0.006, -0.090 to 0.092). Mean north and south edges both moved north (18.9 and 16.5 km), but in the East only the south edge moved. Of 106 species with both edges inside the network, both-north, both-south, expansion and contraction patterns had similar frequencies. Limitations: no detection model, uneven route coverage, interpolated temperature, and a correlational design. Conclusion: a small general north shift is present, but local warming does not explain its size for each species.
